title: British Vlogger Says Mumbai’s Taj Is in a ‘Different League’ From Pakistan’s Top Hotels
excerpt: Travel content creator Harry Jaggard compared stays at Mumbai’s Taj Mahal Palace and Karachi’s Pearl Continental, calling Indian five-star hotels comparable to the best in Dubai and the UK.
body:
• British travel vlogger Harry Jaggard said Mumbai’s Taj Mahal Palace delivered a five-star experience on par with luxury properties in Dubai and the UK.
  • Jaggard described Karachi’s Pearl Continental as “nowhere near” the standard of Indian five-star hotels, saying a top-rated stay in Pakistan could feel closer to a three- or four-star experience.
  • His comments, made on the Holafy podcast, have gone viral and reignited debate about how hotel star ratings vary by market and whether social media reviews are reshaping travel expectations.

A British travel vlogger’s unvarnished comparison of luxury hotels in India and Pakistan has gone viral after he declared that Mumbai’s Taj Mahal Palace operates in “a different league” from the top-rated properties he experienced in Karachi.

Harry Jaggard made the remarks during an appearance on the Holafy podcast, where he spoke at length about his stays across South Asia. His assessment was blunt: Indian five-star hotels deliver genuine five-star experiences, while comparable ratings in Pakistan and Bangladesh can mask significantly lower standards.

‘An Unbelievable Property’

Jaggard was particularly effusive about the Taj Mahal Palace in Mumbai, calling it an “unbelievable property” and praising the quality of service, dining, and overall atmosphere. The hotel, located near the Gateway of India, has been operating since 1903 and remains one of the Taj Hotels chain’s flagship properties. It positions itself as a heritage luxury destination built around personalised service and its historic waterfront setting.

“Indian five-star hotels are actually five-star. A five-star stay in Pakistan or Bangladesh could feel closer to a four-star or even three-star experience.”

— Harry Jaggard, travel vlogger

His experience at Karachi’s Pearl Continental, which he described as one of the city’s leading hotels, drew a sharply different verdict. Jaggard said the property was “nowhere near” the standard he had encountered at Indian hotels, a gap he attributed to differences in market maturity and consumer expectations rather than any lack of effort.

India’s Luxury Hospitality Boom

What stood out most in Jaggard’s comments was not the comparison itself but his broader assessment of India’s luxury market. He argued that Indian five-star properties now offer hospitality comparable to what he has experienced in Dubai and the UK — a shift he linked to India’s growing wealth, expanding middle class, and a generation of consumers willing to pay for premium experiences.

The observation aligns with broader industry trends. India’s luxury hospitality sector has attracted significant international investment in recent years, with global chains expanding their footprints alongside homegrown brands like Taj, Oberoi, and ITC. Mumbai, in particular, has long maintained a deep bench of established luxury properties that cater to both business and leisure travellers.

Star Ratings and the Social Media Effect

Jaggard’s comments have sparked considerable discussion online, partly because hotel star ratings are not standardised globally. A five-star designation in one country may reflect different criteria than in another, making direct comparisons inherently imperfect. His assessment was based on personal experience rather than any formal audit of either country’s hotel industry.

The viral response, however, points to a broader shift in how luxury travel is evaluated. Increasingly, first-hand accounts shared through podcasts, YouTube, and social media carry as much weight with prospective travellers as official ratings or guidebook reviews. A single vlogger’s verdict can reach millions and shape perceptions in ways that traditional hospitality marketing cannot easily counter.

What It Means for Travellers

For travellers planning trips to South Asia, the takeaway is less about which country has better hotels and more about calibrating expectations. India’s major cities — Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore, Udaipur — now host luxury properties that genuinely compete with the world’s best. Pakistan’s hospitality sector, while improving, operates in a different stage of development. As Jaggard’s experience suggests, star ratings alone may not tell the full story.
